The probability ratio

Data costs time to collect. PPO collects a batch with the old policy, then reuses it to score many candidate new policies. Each sample is weighted by the probability ratio $r = \pi_{\text{new}} / \pi_{\text{old}}$: how much more often the new policy would take that action.

The maths

For a sample $(s_t, a_t)$ collected by $\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}$, the probability ratio is

$$r_t(\theta) = \frac{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(a_t \mid s_t)}, \qquad r_t(\theta_{\text{old}}) = 1$$

$r_t > 1$ means the new policy takes that action more often than the old one did; $r_t < 1$ means less often.

Importance sampling (Lesson 39) turns an average under the new policy into one under the old:

$$\begin{aligned} \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_{\text{old}}}\big[r(a)\,A(a)\big] &= \sum_a \pi_{\text{old}}(a)\,\frac{\pi_{\text{new}}(a)}{\pi_{\text{old}}(a)}\,A(a) \\ &= \mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_{\text{new}}}\big[A(a)\big] \end{aligned}$$

So old data can score the new policy's average advantage. PPO's starting point is this surrogate objective (Schulman et al. 2017, eq. 6), with $\hat A_t$ the advantage estimate from Lesson 78:

$$L^{\text{CPI}}(\theta) = \hat{\mathbb{E}}_t\big[r_t(\theta)\,\hat A_t\big]$$

$\hat{\mathbb{E}}_t$ is an average over the batch. "CPI" stands for conservative policy iteration (Kakade and Langford, 2002).

Its gradient at the old policy is the policy gradient. Since $\nabla_\theta\, r_t = \nabla_\theta \pi_\theta / \pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}$,

$$\begin{aligned} \nabla_\theta L^{\text{CPI}}\big|_{\theta = \theta_{\text{old}}} &= \hat{\mathbb{E}}_t\!\left[\frac{\nabla_\theta \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}{\pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)}\,\hat A_t\right] \\ &= \hat{\mathbb{E}}_t\big[\nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta(a_t \mid s_t)\,\hat A_t\big] \end{aligned}$$

One gradient step on $L^{\text{CPI}}$ is an ordinary actor-critic step. The difference is that $L^{\text{CPI}}$ can be optimised for several steps on the same batch.

When the surrogate is exact. In a bandit there is one state and $A(a) = q(a) - J_{\text{old}}$, so

$$\sum_a \pi_{\text{new}}(a)\big(q(a) - J_{\text{old}}\big) = J_{\text{new}} - J_{\text{old}}$$

That is why the two numbers above always agree. In an MDP the new policy also visits different states, which the surrogate ignores. TRPO's Theorem 1 (Schulman et al. 2015) bounds the error. With discount $\gamma$, $\rho_{\text{old}}$ the discounted state visit counts of the old policy and $\varepsilon_A = \max_{s,a}|A_{\text{old}}(s,a)|$,

$$\begin{aligned} J(\pi_{\text{new}}) \ \ge\ J(\pi_{\text{old}}) &+ \sum_s \rho_{\text{old}}(s) \sum_a \pi_{\text{new}}(a \mid s)\,A_{\text{old}}(s,a) \\ &- \frac{4\varepsilon_A\gamma}{(1-\gamma)^2}\,\max_s D_{\mathrm{KL}}\big(\pi_{\text{old}}(\cdot \mid s)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{new}}(\cdot \mid s)\big) \end{aligned}$$

Improve the surrogate while keeping the KL small, and the true return is guaranteed to improve.

The estimate gets noisy far from the old policy. The second moment of each term is

$$\mathbb{E}_{a \sim \pi_{\text{old}}}\big[(r A)^2\big] = \sum_a \frac{\pi_{\text{new}}(a)^2}{\pi_{\text{old}}(a)}\,A(a)^2$$

Putting much more weight on an action the old policy rarely took makes $\pi_{\text{new}}^2 / \pi_{\text{old}}$ large, and the dots spread out. Either reason says the same thing: trust the surrogate only near $r = 1$.
